highlights.title: Who’s behind the new ‘stealth model’ Ox Alpha?
highlights.summary: A mysterious new AI model called Ox Alpha has driven certain corners of the internet into a frenzy of speculation.
body: The free model was released on OpenRouter on Thursday, where it was described as “a reasoning model designed for coding, sustained agentic work, and production workload.” On X, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison (whose company is acquiring OpenRouter ) described Ox Alpha as “very impressive.”

So who’s actually behind Ox Alpha? The OpenRouter listing described it as a “stealth model” and said it was “developed and operated by a third-party provider who has chosen to remain anonymous during this preview.”

Unsurprisingly, much of the speculation has revolved around China. AI analyst Andrew Curran posted on Friday that the initial speculation focused on the GLM models developed by Chinese company Z.ai, but “this morning people seem less sure of anything.”

Similarly, an article on Wccftech first suggested that the evidence pointed to GLM, but an update suggested that Ox Alpha could be an unreleased version of Microsoft’s MAI. And on Reddit, there’s at least one post declaring that Ox Alpha “can’t be the Chinese,” while another expressed “high confidence” that it is, in fact, Chinese.

highlights.title: Meet the Filipino tennis superstar-in-waiting with a punch to rival Pacquiao's
highlights.summary: "Once it grows, it cannot be stopped" - tennis superstar-in-the-making Alex Eala is quickly becoming the biggest thing to come out of the Philippines since legendary boxer Manny Pacquiao.
body: The 21-year-old is carrying the hopes of a nation, the volume of support when she plays calling to mind the days when world boxing champion 'Pac Man' put the country on the map as a sporting force.

Few young players on the WTA Tour have experienced the level of expectation and support Eala has received ‌since she earned a place on the circuit, and she showed what all the fuss is about ‌by winning the recent Washington Open.

After a run to the fourth round of Wimbledon, which included a victory over defending champion Iga Swiatek, Eala capped her breakthrough in the US capital by rallying to defeat top seed Jessica Pegula 4-6 ​6-4 6-0 in a rain-interrupted final, becoming the first woman from her country to claim a tour-level singles crown.
Along the way, ​she beat Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen, last year's winner Leylah ‌Fernandez, second seed Elina Svitolina and four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka.

body: This initial stage is mainly limited to players who pre-ordered the full game, though free beta codes from content creators, social media giveaways, and other sources have been available if you knew where to look. It's worth keeping that in mind before we begin, as that essentially limits the beta's reach, and could mean larger numbers next weekend when the open portion kicks off.

Notably, the Modern Warfare 4 beta has its own entry on Steam, and doesn't live under the Call of Duty app.

The full game may yet exist under that app, which would make it harder to track its performance, as the Call of Duty app also includes free-to-play Warzone as well as several of the past years' games.

highlights.title: ‘Everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place’: Brescia, Lombardy’s hidden gem
highlights.summary: The city’s rich history and culture have so far flown under the radar, but its fiercely proud inhabitants are determined to change that. We have hardly begun walking before I spot the side alley, curving away from the main road in a patchwork of sunlit yellow walls, shuttered windows and shadowy…
body: I turn up the alley. There’s a lot of graffiti. Next to an anarchy symbol, someone has sprayed “ morte al decoro ” – death to decorum. I’m intrigued. We go further, finding a labyrinth of colourful streets filled with bars and restaurants, a few just opening up for the day.

Like the bohemian quarter at its heart, Brescia is an Italian city that is easily missed: it’s near the Dolomites and Lake Garda, but not close enough to be a base for them. Tourists tend to speed past on their way to Milan or Verona. Fiercely proud of her city, Elena is on a mission to convince me it is worth a stop. “You’ll see. We’ve got everything you’d want from Italy, all in one place.”

Her confidence is matched by Andrea, the manager of i Dù dela Contrada, a Carmine bar that we step into for a coffee. Quirky bric-a-brac is dotted around, the bar itself plastered with passport photos, donated by its many fans. “Twenty years ago, this was an area for prostitutes and thieves,” Andrea tells me. “Now it’s safer but still vibrant, and growing.”
I tell him Elena’s mission and he nods. “She’s right, ask anyone.”

highlights.title: Linkdaze’s smart calendar is built to run a household, not just track a schedule
highlights.summary: Linkdaze's smart digital calendar stands out for not putting its features behind a paywall, including an AI meal planner tool.
body: With back-to-school season approaching (or already here in some places), keeping track of everyone’s schedules can get pretty chaotic. Between work, school, appointments, sports, chores, and everything else going on, a regular paper calendar just doesn’t cut it. That’s where Linkdaze’s smart digital calendar comes in — a touchscreen tablet built specifically to organize a household rather than a single person.

One of Linkdaze’s biggest strengths is its calendar compatibility. The system can synchronize calendars from popular services, including Google, iCloud, Outlook, Yahoo, and Cozi, which is a dedicated family-organizing app. This is particularly useful for families where different members use different platforms. Instead of asking everyone to switch to a single calendar app, Linkdaze brings multiple schedules together and uses color coding to make individual family members easy to identify.

highlights.title: My Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territory
highlights.summary: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb. Most stealth games cast you as a spy, an assassin or a master thief.
body: As Toot Games co-founder Matthew Jackson puts it: “You are the bad thing that happens to the people.”

The idea began as a much simpler prototype made during a weekend game jam themed around the idea of lost and found. Jackson and fellow Toot co-founder Millie Holten, who met through Melbourne’s improv and sketch comedy community, wanted an idea that could be understood – and raise a laugh – in a single still image. A grotesquely extended arm proved to be just that.

Since then, the game has been all about comedy. It has more than 40 speaking characters, voiced by Australian comedians who perform the written dialogue before improvising alternative takes. “It’s a vessel for jokes,” Jackson says. For almost a year, development largely involved trying to “cram jokes into the game”; only later did the team realise the physics of the increasingly sophisticated arm had become fun in their own right. Players can personalise its skin tone, hair and accessories, making it less somebody else’s disembodied crime spree than a freaky extension of their own body.

highlights.title: Netflix's 5 Biggest Sci-Fi Flops, Ranked by Their Rotten Tomatoes Scores
highlights.summary: Netflix has become the streaming equivalent of a giant video store. Whether you're looking for an Oscar-winning drama, a true-crime documentary, a reality dating show, or an action blockbuster, chances are you'll find something worth watching.
body: But Netflix has also spent hundreds of millions of dollars on ambitious original sci-fi movies that arrived with blockbuster aspirations only to vanish from the cultural conversation before the streamer could even ask, "Are you still watching?" Whether they suffered from weak scripts, impossible expectations, or simply failed to leave much of an impression, these are Netflix's five biggest sci-fi flops.

Anthony Mackie and Margaret Qualley headline this post-apocalyptic drama set after Earth has become largely uninhabitable. Qualley plays Sam, one of the last humans still living on the planet while waiting for the final spacecraft bound for humanity's off-world colony on Io, one of Jupiter's moons. When another survivor (Mackie) arrives, the two find themselves divided over whether humanity's future lies among the stars or in trying to adapt to the world they already have.

highlights.title: A new start after 60: I became a grocer – and feel stronger physically and quieter mentally
highlights.summary: Robert Solomon loves the early mornings, picking out the apples, tending to the broccoli and fussing up the dandelion greens. At 71, he says it’s the best job he’s had.
body: When Robert Solomon’s working hours were cut during the pandemic – he did building management and tech support for a nonprofit organisation – he got an extra job at a food cooperative, helping to stock the store. It was, he says, the most ordinary job, but that’s what made it special.

That job ended with the pandemic, but in 2022 he left the nonprofit and hunted for grocery positions. Now, at 71, he is assistant buyer in produce (ie fruit and vegetables) at an independent market in New York. “I love the opportunity to do physical, creative work with my body, hands and mind,” he says. “I’m working harder than I have since my 30s, and I love it.”

Solomon’s favourite time of day is the morning. He often starts at 5.30am or 6am. “I put the rugs back on the floor and the carts out in the yard. And then I start stocking.” Certain products make him particularly happy.

highlights.title: Flock CEO calls for ‘compromise’ as surveillance company faces growing backlash
highlights.summary: Flock Safety faces a growing public outcry over concerns that its surveillance technology could be misused.
body: The country needs to find a “compromise” between privacy and safety, according to Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley.

“When people talk about just one of these, privacy or safety, they’re prioritizing the wrong thing, and what we have to prioritize as a country is compromise,” Langley said during a recent interview with Fox News. “How do we have our safety, and how do we balance privacy?”

Langley’s Fox News appearance was just the latest interview he’s given as the company faces a growing public outcry around concerns that Flock’s surveillance cameras, drones, and license plate recognition technology could be misused.

These concerns aren’t just hypothetical. The Washington Post recently identified 46 cases where police officers have been accused of using Flock technology for unauthorized purposes, including to stalk their wives, girlfriends, or exes.

body: This kraut can be used much like traditional sauerkraut, though its flavour is milder and its texture more delicate. Sauteed with onions in a little butter or lard, it makes an excellent accompaniment to roast meats and sausages; it can also be added to potato pancakes or used as a filling for savoury pies and pastries.
Wash the unpeeled courgettes and pat them dry. Cut the courgettes in half lengthways, scrape out the seeds and shred or coarsely grate the flesh into a bowl.

Mix the sugar, salt and vinegar, then pour this over the courgettes. Sprinkle in the caraway seeds, mix well and set aside for 15-30 minutes. Adjust the seasoning to taste, adding sugar or vinegar as required.

highlights.title: Is it legal to train AI models on copyrighted books? It’s complicated
highlights.summary: Most published authors have, without their knowledge or consent, contributed to the development of the same AI tools that threaten to undermine their livelihoods. That seems illegal, right?
body: “I think one of the issues with this entire area of law and this entire area of technology is there’s a lot going on,” Cathy Gellis, an attorney with expertise in intellectual property, copyright, and technology, told TechCrunch. “It’s very complex and there are a lot of raw feelings about what is happening, both for and against.”

Last year, in one of the first rulings of its kind, Judge William Alsup ordered Anthropic to pay a mammoth $1.5 billion copyright settlement to a group of writers whose works were used to train the company’s AI models. At face value, this seemed like a moral victory favoring authors, but Judge Alsup actually ruled that Anthropic’s AI training was lawful. What Alsup penalized Anthropic for was pirating these books from illegal online shadow libraries.

“Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” the judge wrote, comparing the way an LLM ingests trillions of words to a writer’s study of literature.

highlights.title: Disciples review – fresh-faced boys are sucked into a nightmare of extremism in India
highlights.summary: A prestigious school in the holy city of Varanasi and its controversial, dogmatic teachings are the subject of this shocking documentary. The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison.
body: The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.

For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.

highlights.title: The Unlikely Place at the Center of China’s AI Boom
highlights.summary: Cheap energy, abundant land, and proximity to Beijing have turned a city in Inner Mongolia into a crucial hub for data centers.
body: Travel just two hours west of Beijing by train, and you’ll find yourself surrounded by the rolling grasslands and ancient cinder cones of Inner Mongolia. This vast, arid land has long been China’s capital of sheep farming and coal mining, but over the last few years, it has become the hottest place in the country to build an AI data center.

In Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia home to about 1.5 million people, nearly 100 data centers have been opened or begun construction since 2016. Chinese companies have pledged to build projects with a combined estimated capacity of 12.5 gigawatts in the city, and over 70 percent of the total commitments have been announced in just the last year, making it one of the fastest growing compute clusters in Asia, according to a research note published by Goldman Sachs last week. For comparison, OpenAI’s $500 billion Stargate Project is set to reach only 10 gigawatts of total capacity when it’s complete.

highlights.summary: Full spoilers follow for HBO’s Lanterns Episode 2. After last week’s premiere episode of Lanterns – the latest show in James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Universe – got some fans fuming and others interested thanks to the radical decision to kill off legendary Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler)…
body: At first glance, this show could be confused with being just another detective series set in smalltown USA. But then a scene like the one that ends Episode 2 happens, and there’s no doubt that this is the space cop Green Lantern, a guy who can fly to another planet at the drop of a hat.

“It's like Kyle says in the bar in the pilot, ‘When and where to use the ring is the whole ballgame,’” showrunner Chris Mundy told me when I asked him about the use of the Green Lantern ring on the show. For him and his team, the decision on when to use it, and when not to use it, was not taken lightly.

“That was a character thing for Hal, but it was also sort of us talking to ourselves a little bit,” he continued. “We wanted to earn the times we used it in a big way. We start small and start kind of playful with the $20 bill and all those kinds of things, so that each time we used it, people trusted us, like, ‘Oh, they're not just plastering everything with it all the time.’ It's those characters [deciding when to use it], and then because of that, those writers who are making those characters do that thing, they know when to employ it and when not to.”

highlights.title: Clash Royale research finds 85% of rage quitters enjoy gaming more after returning
highlights.summary: Supercell has revealed that 85.1% of rage quitters say they enjoy gaming more when they come back. That's according to research commissioned by Clash Royale, which surveyed 9,000 gamers across seven markets as the mobile game searches for a player to become its first-ever rage emote.... [ MORE ]
body: The research found that Mexico had the highest share of players who enjoyed the game more after returning from a rage quit, at 90.5%, while Germany recorded the lowest at 74.4%.

Globally, gamers said they rage quit because they want to do well (31.1%), care about the game (22.1%) and want to protect a winning streak (21.9%). Brazil had the highest share of gamers who had rage quit, at 77%, compared with 59% in Mexico.

The research also found that close to four in 10 gamers who rage quit have done so somewhere public. The US was the only market where gamers wanted an audience, with 55.6% of US rage quitters saying they would happily post a clip of the moment.
In the UK, 31.5% of public rage quitters had done so in a pub, while British gamers also led in ranting to a friend at 20.8% and screaming into a pillow at 17.2%.

Surrounded by relatives, memories and inherited ideas of love and parenthood, Hoda and Boris begin to question the roles they are about to take on. What starts as a plan to become a family gradually opens into a more intimate and uncertain question: can they reinvent what it means to be a couple without losing what brought them together?”

highlights.title: Are Creators Up to the Task of Their New Marketing Roles?
highlights.summary: The creator job description is no longer limited to making and distributing content — influencers are now expected to have business savvy to boot.
body: For over 70 years, the Cannes Lions festival has welcomed marketing and advertising suits to the South of France for a week of schmoozing and dealmaking. In recent years, though, a new crowd has descended on the French Riviera: influencers. And in 2026, they were front and center, speaking on panels, attending lunches, dinners and parties, and taking meetings along the Croisette.
For some, it was the farthest they’d gone into the business side of content marketing. Cannes may be a fabulous setting for a conference, but it’s a conference nonetheless.

For most influencers, they’ve built followings online because they’re funny or aspirational, not because of their business savvy. Now, brands more often want them to take on the role of representatives at industry events — and to contribute to marketing strategies back home.

“The role of an influencer/creator in 2026 looks very different from what it was,” says influencer marketing agency Ponte Firm founder Shana Davis. Caroline Wilson, an executive in UTA’s brand advisory group, refers to creators as “a marketing strategy” in and of themselves, as opposed to a prong or add-on in a larger marketing machine separate from them.

highlights.title: After more than 15 years of laptops in the classroom, do Australian schools need a rethink?
highlights.summary: ‘We don’t want distraction, we want concentration’: many teachers and parent groups think its time for a ‘digital detox’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates. Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
body: Earlier this month, the federal education minister, Jason Clare, took to Facebook. “When I was a kid there was a computer room at school. Now they are everywhere. From morning till night,” he wrote. “I think there is a good argument our kids need a digital detox.”
Since that post, as the minister told ABC News Breakfast last week, he has been “inundated” with support from parents and teachers.

Clare’s comments followed the Victorian government’s announcement that it will abolish the use of bring your own device (BYOD) programs in primary schools and limit screen use to 90 minutes per day for years 3 to 6 from January next year. High schools have been instructed to enforce screen-free learning blocks for all students. The then premier Jacinta Allen launched the policy in July, saying: “Less time on devices means more time learning.”

Computer use has expanded rapidly in schools in Australia and worldwide. “Computer rooms” like those in Clare’s days have been replaced by a laptop in most high school students’ backpacks, touted more than 15 years ago as the “toolbox of the 21st century” and essential to equipping students with the skills they would need for the future.

body: LinkedIn’s new AI slop button is apparently getting a lot of use.

LinkedIn announced the button a few weeks after AI detector Pangram determined that 41 percent of LinkedIn’s longform posts were flagged as fully AI generated, which 404 Media reported on. highlights.title: HBO Officially Changes a Fundamental Rule of DC Superhero Canon
highlights.summary: In 2014’s Justice League: War, heroes including Superman, Wonder Woman, and the Flash unite to defend Earth from an invasion led by Darkseid. Batman and Green Lantern are among the first to stumble into an uneasy partnership.
body: Adapted from Geoff Johns and Jim Lee’s 2011 Justice League #1, the scene is a funny distillation of both characters. Hal is powerful and cocky. Batman is observant enough to identify and steal the source of that power within minutes. It also dramatizes one of the Green Lantern mythology’s basic rules: The ring transforms willpower into physical hard-light constructs, but a Lantern has to be wearing the ring to wield that power.
HBO’s Lanterns just pushed that rule to its apparent limit — and potentially set John Stewart up to become the most powerful Green Lantern in the DC Universe.

In Lanterns episode 2, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) maintains an intricate, autonomous construct while separated from the ring and after repeatedly losing consciousness. The Green Lantern comics contain a handful of comparable feats, but they usually involve veteran Lanterns, unusual rings, or cosmic transformations. John accomplishes it after just two months of training, which already makes him seem like a prodigy among the Corps.

highlights.title: In Luxury’s New Resale Era, Everyone’s a Fashion Expert
highlights.summary: The RealReal’s 2026 resale report illustrates the rise in specificity and saviness in luxury resale. This will change how the industry operates.
body: Gone are the days of simply searching names like “Prada” on resale sites and scrolling away. In 2026, shoppers are getting ultra-specific with their secondhand marketplace searches, a shift that has wider implications for the resale industry.

“The hyper-specificity of the way that people search really stands out as a fundamental shift in the way people think about shopping,” says Kristen Naiman, chief brand officer at luxury online resale marketplace The RealReal. “The fact that people are searching for not just ‘Prada 2010’, but ‘Prada 2010 linen’ or ‘Chanel 2013, look 31’ tells me they have developed both a fluency around style and fashion, as well as an emphasis on singularity and one-of-oneness.”

This was one of the key takeaways of The RealReal’s 2026 resale report, which takes stock of the biggest shifts and developments in the secondhand market. The root of the shift is two-pronged, Naiman says: people want more unique clothes, and they want to invest in items they can make a return from down the line. Forty-seven percent of shoppers actively evaluate an item’s potential resale value before making a purchase in the primary market.
